scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that time clarifies greatness, then argues contemporaries can recognise it too; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: History is full of artists and thinkers who were ignored in their lifetimes and celebrated only after death.
Some people argue that the greatness of individuals can be judged only by later generations, never by their own contemporaries.
I agree that time often clarifies who was truly great, but I do not believe that contemporaries are completely unable to recognise greatness.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why later generations judge well

sentences.text: First, later generations often see a person's greatness more clearly than the people who lived alongside her.
Time reveals the lasting effects of someone's work, which may be invisible while that person is still alive.
For example, the painter Vincent van Gogh sold almost nothing in his life, yet is now regarded as one of the greatest artists in history.
This shows that contemporaries can be blinded by fashion, jealousy, or a simple failure to understand new ideas.
Distance also frees later judges from the rivalries and politics that distort opinion in a person's own time.
Only the passage of years can show whether an achievement truly endures or quickly fades away.
In this respect, posterity often does deliver the fairer verdict.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why contemporaries can judge too

sentences.text: Second, however, it is simply not true that contemporaries can never recognise greatness.
Many of the most celebrated figures in history were honoured and admired during their own lifetimes.
Consider leaders like Nelson Mandela or scientists like Albert Einstein, whose greatness was widely acknowledged while they still lived.
Their example shows that people are often perfectly able to see greatness as it unfolds around them.
Waiting only for later generations would also leave us unable to praise or learn from great people in the present.
Later judges, moreover, carry their own biases and can misjudge the past as easily as contemporaries misjudge the present.
Greatness, then, can be recognised both in a person's own time and long after it.
In conclusion, later generations often judge greatness more clearly than those who lived at the same time.
But contemporaries are far from blind, and many great people are honoured during their own lives.
The truest measure of greatness comes not from one age alone, but from the agreement of both the present and the future.
